analysis.one_liner: Keeps Social Security checks flowing if trust funds run short, with solvency fixes funded by the ultra-wealthy.
analysis.headline: The bill sits in the House Ways and Means Committee with one sponsor and zero cosponsors, with no action since its February referral.
analysis.plain_summary: If a Social Security trust fund ever runs out of money, this bill orders the Treasury to keep paying full benefits every month, no matter what. It also fast-tracks any bill that fixes the funding gap, with strict rules: benefits must stay whole, the bill cannot cut benefits or raise taxes on ordinary earners, and any new money must come from ultra-wealthy households and corporations. It also requires a Social Security field office in every U.S. county with more than 150,000 people.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries — nearly 9 out of 10 people age 65 and older receive benefits, and over 6 million children depend on them. If the trust fund were insufficient, current law would trigger automatic cuts of roughly one-fifth of benefits; this bill guarantees full payments instead.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security beneficiaries and their families

how_it_helps.text: Requires automatic monthly appropriations to an insolvent trust fund equal to whatever is needed to keep paying full benefits.

Fast-tracks a solvency bill once the Social Security Commissioner certifies insolvency: committees must report within 5 days or be discharged, debate is capped (10 hours in the Senate, 2 in the House), amendments are barred, and Senate procedures that normally let a minority block a bill with endless debate are waived.
Any fast-tracked solvency bill must keep benefits fully intact and cannot raise taxes on anyone other than the ultra-wealthy and corporations, who must bear any added cost.
Requires the Social Security Administration to operate a field office in every county with a population above 150,000, so beneficiaries who cannot use online or phone services have in-person help.

analysis.who_pays: Ultra-wealthy households and corporations, whose taxes would fund any solvency bill under the bill's requirements, and the general Treasury, which backstops monthly benefit payments in the meantime.

drawbacks.text: The field office requirement covers only counties with more than 150,000 residents, so smaller counties get no guaranteed office.
The expedited procedure bars all amendments in both chambers and caps debate, so even a solvency bill with drafting flaws could not be changed once triggered.
The bill never defines "ultra-wealthy" or "corporations," leaving the key question of who exactly pays to future legislation.
The protections switch on only after the trust fund is already short; the bill does not fix the long-term financing gap before that point.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For beneficiaries the core promise is strong and direct: an automatic backstop means their checks never shrink, even if the trust fund's accounting runs out. The costs fall on the people and firms asked to fund a fix, and the no-amendment, short-debate procedure sacrifices flexibility for speed. The undefined "ultra-wealthy" standard is a real drafting gap. On balance, a plainly pro-beneficiary bill with a coarse, partisan-flavored process attached.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2025 and referred to the House Ways and Means and Rules committees, where it has sat ever since.

narrative.text: Rep. Patrick Ryan introduced the bill on February 4, 2025, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Rules Committee.
No further action has been taken, and the bill has no cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has happened yet — the bill has not moved, so neither beneficiaries nor anyone else has gained or lost. The safest read so far is that the status quo, where trust fund insolvency would trigger automatic benefit cuts, remains in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No outcome yet — bill is pending

for.name: Rep. Patrick Ryan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Ways and Means and Rules committees.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party; the bill's own findings name President Trump and Republican congressional leaders as threats to Social Security, and it has drawn no Republican support.

industries.note: If the fast-track is ever triggered, any new funding must come from them, so they would bear the cost of keeping Social Security solvent. Their gain — avoiding those taxes — would come at beneficiaries' expense.
The bill mandates a field office in every county over 150,000 people, requiring an expansion of local offices, while also giving the agency a new reporting duty on insolvency.

analysis.trajectory: With one sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no committee action since February, this bill follows the common path of a messaging bill: it will likely stay in Ways and Means and expire at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote unless other members sign on and leadership decides to move it.
